title: Acute aortic syndrome and aortic dissection
subject: cardiology
setting: Emergency department, ICU, cardiothoracic or vascular centre
summary: Suspect aortic dissection in any severe abrupt chest, back or abdominal pain; use the ADD-RS with D-dimer and urgent CT angiography, give IV opioid and IV beta-blocker to heart rate below 60/min and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg, send type A for emergency surgery and treat uncomplicated type B medically with TEVAR for complications.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Acute aortic syndrome includes classic dissection, intramural haematoma, penetrating aortic ulcer and aortic rupture. Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta; type B does not.

Typical pain: abrupt, severe, tearing or stabbing chest, back or abdominal pain, maximal at onset, sometimes migrating. It may be painless, especially in the elderly, and may present as syncope, stroke, limb ischaemia or paraplegia.

Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (1 point per category): high-risk conditions (Marfan or other connective tissue disease, family history of aortic disease, known aortic valve disease or thoracic aneurysm, recent aortic manipulation); high-risk pain features; high-risk examination features (pulse deficit or BP difference between arms, focal neurological deficit with pain, new aortic regurgitation murmur with pain, hypotension or shock).

Complications to look for: aortic regurgitation, tamponade, coronary involvement (usually inferior STEMI from the right coronary artery), stroke, mesenteric, renal or limb malperfusion, rupture (haemothorax).

sections.title: Investigations
items: ADD-RS 0 or 1 (low or intermediate probability): D-dimer. Below 500 ng/mL makes AAS unlikely; consider alternative diagnoses. Positive D-dimer, or ADD-RS 2 or 3: urgent imaging.
CT angiography of the whole aorta (chest, abdomen and pelvis, ECG-gated where available) is the first-line test in stable patients.
Unstable patient: bedside transthoracic echo (flap, aortic regurgitation, pericardial effusion) and transoesophageal echo in theatre or ICU; do not transfer for CT if it delays surgery.
ECG (ischaemia, LVH), troponin, CBC, group and crossmatch, creatinine, lactate, coagulation. Chest X-ray may show a wide mediastinum but a normal film does not exclude dissection.

sections.title: Immediate management
items: Two large-bore IV lines, arterial line in the arm with the higher BP, urinary catheter, ICU level monitoring.
IV opioid analgesia (for example morphine titrated) because pain drives tachycardia and hypertension.

Impulse control first: IV beta-blocker (esmolol or labetalol) to heart rate below 60/min, then target SBP 100 to 120 mmHg, adding a vasodilator (nitroprusside, nicardipine or nitroglycerin) only after beta-blockade.
If beta-blockers are contraindicated (asthma, severe AV block): IV diltiazem or verapamil for rate control.

Hypotension or shock: suspect tamponade, rupture or aortic regurgitation. Do not do pericardiocentesis for tamponade except as a bridge in extremis (small controlled aspirations); go straight to surgery.
Do not give thrombolysis, antiplatelets or anticoagulants until dissection is excluded.

sections.title: Definitive treatment
items: Type A dissection (and type A intramural haematoma): emergency surgery; immediate referral to a cardiothoracic surgical centre. Without surgery, about half of patients die within 48 hours.
Uncomplicated type B: medical therapy with impulse control, pain relief and serial imaging in ICU or HDU; TEVAR may be considered in the subacute phase for high-risk anatomical features.
Complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or hypertension, rapid expansion): TEVAR is the treatment of choice; open surgery if TEVAR is not feasible.
Penetrating aortic ulcer and intramural haematoma follow the same principles, with intervention for ascending involvement or complications.

sections.title: Monitoring and follow-up
items: Continuous heart rate, arterial BP, urine output, limb pulses, neurology (spinal cord ischaemia) and abdominal examination for malperfusion; repeat lactate and creatinine.
Repeat CT for new symptoms or signs, and before discharge in medically treated type B dissection.
Long term: BP below 130/80 mmHg with a beta-blocker as part of therapy; regular imaging follow-up (CT or MRI), most intensive in the first year, planned by the aortic team.
Genetic evaluation and family screening for young patients and those with a family history or syndromic features (for example Marfan).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving thrombolysis or dual antiplatelets for an inferior STEMI caused by dissection: check for pulse deficit, aortic regurgitation and widened mediastinum first.
Starting a vasodilator before beta-blockade (reflex tachycardia increases aortic wall stress).
Relying on a normal chest X-ray or a single BP measurement from one arm.
Delaying transfer of type A dissection for non-essential tests.

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.dose: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg IV bolus over 1 minute, then 50 to 300 mcg/kg/min infusion
drugs.notes: First choice for rapid, titratable heart rate control.

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.dose: 20 mg IV over 2 minutes, then 40 to 80 mg every 10 minutes (maximum cumulative 300 mg), or IV infusion starting at 2 mg/min, titrated

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 2 minutes, repeat every 5 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg

drugs.name: Sodium nitroprusside
drugs.dose: 0.3 to 10 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, titrated to SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
drugs.notes: Only after beta-blockade. Cyanide toxicity with prolonged or high-dose use.

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.dose: 5 mg/h IV, increase by 2.5 mg/h every 15 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg/h

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.dose: 0.25 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, then 5 to 15 mg/h infusion
drugs.notes: Rate control when beta-blockers are contraindicated.

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.dose: 2 to 5 mg IV, titrated every 5 to 10 minutes to pain relief
drugs.notes: Watch for respiratory depression and hypotension.
